item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott.
- Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon.
SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win three consecutive World Series championships since the New York Yankees, from 1998 to 2000.
Those Yankees had a Hall of Fame closer. In 1998, Mariano Rivera got the final four outs of the clincher. In 1999, he got the final four outs. In 2000, he got the final three outs.
These Dodgers? Their closer? Your guess is as good as theirs.
“I do not know,” said Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations.
This might be a good time to know, no? The regular season is over. The postseason is upon us.
Alex Call hits a run-scoring double and Andy Pages follows with a three-run home run in the 10th inning of the Dodgers’ 5-1 win over the San Francisco Giants.
“I feel very confident that we’re going to be going into October with arguably the deepest and best pitching staff that we’ve had,” he said. “Exactly what their roles will be and how things will be ordered, I don’t know right now.”
Perhaps the Dodgers are overthinking this. They have done that before.
Tanner Scott converted 25 of 29 save opportunities this season, including saves Friday and Saturday.
But the strongest hitters on the Dodgers’ possible division series opponents are left-handed — Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II on the Atlanta Braves; Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber on the Philadelphia Phillies — and the Dodgers may not hesitate to use the left-handed Scott against those guys in the seventh or eighth inning.
In theory, these Dodgers have three candidates as closer: Scott, their marquee closer signing for 2025 and actual closer for most of 2026; Edwin Díaz, their marquee closer signing for 2026; and Roki Sasaki, their accidental closer last October.
Yet Friedman said he could envision scenarios where Evan Phillips could close, or even Brock Stewart, or perhaps Alex Vesia against a run of left-handed hitters. The Dodgers hope to activate Edgardo Henriquez for the playoffs. The starters could close, too, especially a well-rested Tyler Glasnow early in the first round.
Dave Roberts know the Dodgers’ chances of a three-peat rest on a surprise hero giving the team a timely boost. Meet Bill Plaschke’s top candidates for the job.
“We’ve got a number of guys that we really trust,” Friedman said. “Depending on who we’re playing, how deep our starter goes, there are a lot of factors that would go into it. But, more than who will be that pitcher on the mound, is the fact that we have so many candidates we feel really good about.”
That the Dodgers have improvised an October relief corps, transformed a rookie starter into a postseason closer and run bullpen games in elimination games might lead you to conclude Friedman does not really believe in the concept of a designated closer. In a world where “high leverage” is the trendy jargon, maybe a closer is more of an anachronism than a necessity.
That the Dodgers invested $72 million in Scott and $69 million in Díaz in consecutive winters would lead you to conclude Friedman does indeed believe in the concept of a designated closer. In fact, he does.
“I think it’s extremely helpful,” he said.
The Dodgers do not hold splashy news conferences to introduce closer candidates. When the Dodgers introduced Díaz last December, Friedman proudly introduced the three-time All-Star as the closer.
“For us, we have a high bar,” Friedman said then. “To name someone the closer, you have to be one of the best. You have to be elite and dominant at what you do.”
Díaz’s season went awry, limited to 18⅔ innings after elbow surgery and then a neck injury. But in five September appearances since his activation from the injured list, he gave up no runs and one hit in five innings, striking out nine of the 17 batters he faced. (In the same span, Scott has given up no runs and two hits in five innings, striking out nine of the 19 batters he faced.)
“What we’ve seen out of Díaz recently has been really encouraging,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “What that ultimately means, we don’t know yet.
“Of course, if you have a reliever who is really hot in October, that can be extremely valuable. It doesn’t mean you use him exclusively in the ninth. But, by and large, that’s how you would use him.”
Roberts saluted Díaz for working hard to get back to an uncertain assignment.
“I’m really proud of Edwin, given the deal he signed, to work it out, to go to the minors, to come back and pitch in whatever role we ask of him, that shows a lot of character,” Roberts said.
“He could have mailed this year in. That’s something that has not gone unnoticed. And we’ll see how October plays out.”
The Dodgers could be forgiven for believing it will all work out in the end. Their final pitcher in each of the World Series clinchers under Friedman, all starters: Julio Urías in 2020, Walker Buehler in 2024, Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025.
The pitchers to record a postseason save in those championship seasons: Kenley Jansen, Joe Kelly, Brusdar Graterol, Blake Treinen and Urias in 2020; Alex Vesia, Treinen and Buehler in 2024; Glasnow, Sasaki and Treinen in 2025.
The organizational flexibility can lead to some uncomfortable discussions within the clubhouse, as Roberts and coaches keep the relievers updated on the latest plan for how they might be used.
“It is tricky,” Roberts said. “These are constant conversations. They are ever-evolving. They are ongoing.”
If all goes right for the Dodgers, those conversations will be ongoing for another month.

item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO — It was a four-inning wellness check.
Pitching for the first time since he left his start in Cincinnati after one inning with groin muscle discomfort, Blake Snell passed his test. He allowed one run on five hits in his four innings Saturday afternoon as the Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants 4-3 on Kiké Hernandez’s ninth-inning home run.
The Dodgers will finish the season with a chance to reach 100 victories for the first time since 2023 – but the fourth time in the past six seasons and sixth time in the past nine full seasons.
Snell was healthy if not efficient. He threw 77 pitches to get through his four innings, allowing hits in each inning.
“Definitely needed to pitch today. Definitely showed that,” Snell said. “I was trying to go up and in, I was missing up and away. Even the last pitch of the game, I try to go up and in and miss right down the middle. I don’t know the last time I did that. It’s been a while. Even the changeup, the speed was up to 88. I gotta fix that as well. Get that to 86. Curveball, the release just has to get better.
“But overall, I learned a lot from it. Really encouraged by it, and just happy to get my legs underneath me and get going and completely move past the groin. I mean, it felt great today, and the velo was good. … I’ve got to figure my body out a little more, but I got a week to do so, and I’m really looking forward to that.”
He stranded runners at the corners in the first inning and at second base in the second. Jonah Cox led off the third with a double into the left-field corner, stole third and scored on a sacrifice fly. Snell gave up a two-out single in the fourth, but Shay Whitcomb was thrown out by left fielder Teoscar Hernandez when he tried to stretch it into a double.
After the game in Cincinnati, Snell expressed confidence that he had avoided serious injury by recognizing the signs early and coming out of the game – something he didn’t do before landing on the injured list four previous times with groin injuries.
Saturday supported that decision. Snell’s fastball averaged 96.8 mph (up slightly from his season average) and he got 10 swings-and-misses (though only three strikeouts). Snell now lines up as the likely Game 3 starter in the National League Division Series, giving him over a week before his next start.
“I thought the fastball was had life. Just some near misses to kind of flip counts,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “The changeup was okay. The curveball I thought was good. But I think for him overall, he just wasn’t as efficient as he wanted, as we wanted. But again, I thought it was fine for his last tune-up for the postseason.
“I was confident, we were confident (that Snell was healthy). But I think it’s still good to see it. And it’s good also that we got it out of the way, got that rust off, versus whatever game in the postseason, then he’s rusty, and you’ve got to kind of pick up the pieces in a playoff game. So I thought today it was again, really best-case scenario.”
The Dodgers’ offense gave Snell a 3-1 lead.
Mookie Betts hit a solo home run in the third inning – his seventh home run in September as he surges over the final month of the season. Four singles and a walk produced two more runs in the fourth inning.
After a two-hit game including an RBI double Thursday, Shohei Ohtani has gone 1 for 9 with five strikeouts in the two games against the Giants. The lone hit was a ground ball under the glove of Giants first baseman Brett Harris in the fourth inning that was originally ruled an error and later changed.
“I thought today there was just more chase,” Roberts said of Ohtani’s 1 for 5. “And I don’t know if he’s trying to get hits, find his swing, getting a little over-anxious. Everything from Shohei to the training staff, the hitting guys, the work has been great. Looks exactly like it did, like it’s supposed to look.”
Roberts dismissed any suggestion that Ohtani is still not healthy after spending two weeks on the injured list.
“I don’t see any wincing. The bat speed is still (good),” Roberts said. “There’s one thing to just say you could just put him on ice and hope that the performance is there Game One of the postseason, or there’s another camp that says everything looks right and you have to get him (at-bats) and it’s still only – what is it 12, 13 at bats, 14 at bats (since he returned)? So, with a long layoff, that’s not easy either to come back and perform.”
The Dodgers’ bullpen couldn’t hold the 3-1 lead. The Giants came back to tie it with single runs against Brock Stewart in the seventh and Evan Phillips in the eighth before Hernandez put the Dodgers back in the lead with a leadoff home run in the ninth.
The homer was an uplifting moment in a difficult season for Hernandez, who started the season on the IL following elbow surgery, returned for two games, then missed two months with an oblique injury.
“Yeah, I mean it’s been tough, but I mean, it is what it is,” Hernandez said. “That’s the card I’ve drawn this year. It’s nobody’s fault. I was expected to miss the first couple months because of my rehab, and then I was not expecting to miss more time so quickly after coming back. It just happened to be that way. And when you have a team like this one, it’s hard getting in the lineup. So it’s just one of those things where that’s what you have, and you got to make the best of it. I just happened to not have made the best of my opportunities this year.”

item.content:encoded:
Blake Snell looked healthy in his final regular season start and Kiké Hernández homered in the ninth inning to give the Dodgers a 4-3 win over the Giants on Saturday afternoon at Oracle Park in San Francisco.
Snell allowed only one run in his four innings and at the very least showed no limitations from leaving his start with left groin tightness on September 16 in Cincinnati. The Dodgers weren’t going to push Snell on Saturday, but more wanted to make sure he got one more start in before the postseason starts in a week.
“If he can go five innings and come out of it feeling great, that would be fantastic,” manager Dave Roberts told reporters at Oracle Park earlier Saturday, as shown on SportsNet LA. “There’s a balance between getting your work in and making sure you feel good coming out of it.”
Snell threw 77 pitches in his four innings so he wasn’t all that efficient, though he didn’t walk anyone and threw his two fastest pitches of the season — first-inning fastballs at 98.6 mph and 98.2 mph — while averaging 96.8 mph on the fastball on Saturday.
The lone run came when Jonah Cox doubled to open the third inning, stole third base, and scored on a sacrifice fly.
San Francisco swiped two bases Saturday off Snell, who has allowed 10 steals in his nine starts this season. But Snell has limited the damage by simply not allowing many people to reach, with only 25 hits and 14 walks in 39 2/3 innings, a .260 on-base percentage since returning from the injured list.
Snell since returning allowed only five runs, never more than one in any start. On the season he did not allow a home run, his 42 2/3 innings the seventh-most by a Dodgers pitcher in the live-ball era without giving up a long ball.
Most Dodgers innings without allowing a home run
| Pitcher | Season | Innings | ERA |
| Jack Billingham | 1968 | 71 1/3 | 2.14 |
| Brandon League | 2014 | 63 | 2.57 |
| Newt Kimball | 1941 | 52 | 3.63 |
| Joe Beimel | 2008 | 49 | 2.02 |
| Dutch Henry | 1924 | 46 | 5.67 |
| Brandon Morrow | 2017 | 43 2/3 | 2.06 |
| Blake Snell | 2026 | 42 2/3 | 1.90 |
Just like last Sunday at Dodger Stadium, the Dodgers did the bulk of their damage after Matt Wilkinson left. The rookie left-hander, who pitched five scoreless innings in Los Angeles before the Dodgers scored single runs in the next three innings to complete a weekend sweep, on Saturday held the Dodgers without a run until Mookie Betts hit one into the left field seats in the third inning.
Betts has seven home runs in September, after hitting five combined home runs in July and August. It’s been a month to remember for Betts, who raised his seasonal OPS from .701 at the start of September to .783 now, with just one day remaining in the regular season.
Wilkinson was done after three innings, and the Dodgers immediately responded with four singles and a walk in the fourth inning to score two runs.
San Francisco clawed back with single runs in the seventh and eighth innings, before Hernández took Trent Harris deep to open the ninth inning.
Treinen hurt?
Brock Stewart pitched the bottom of the seventh inning but was allotted extra warm-up pitches as he entered the game. He wasn’t warming up in the bullpen before getting called in, but Blake Treinen was before suddenly stopping. In the top of the eighth, the SportsNet LA broadcast showed footage from the Dodgers bullpen, showing bullpen coach Josh Bard embracing Treinen, then of Treinen walking back to the Dodgers dugout and clubhouse with trainer Bernard Li.
Treinen missed two and a half months with elbow inflammation before returning in September, when he has allowed three runs in 6 2/3 innings, with three walks and six strikeouts.
Saturday particulars
Home runs: Mookie Betts (23), Kiké Hernández (4)
WP — Evan Phillips (3-2): 1 IP, 1 hit, 1 run, 1 strikeout
LP — Trent Harris (0-1): 1 IP, 2 hits, 1 run
Sv — Tanner Scott (25): 1 IP, 1 hit, 2 strikeouts

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez provided an update on his back injury, which has him on the injured list and makes his postseason status uncertain.
Edgardo Henriquez’s injury progress
Henriquez told The Athletic’s Fabian Aradaya that he threw a bullpen session on Wednesday, September 24th, his first since being placed on the injured list.
He feels like his back is in a better spot, and that he can get ready for the National League Division Series on Saturday, October 3rd.
The Dodgers put Henriquez on the 15-day injured list a little more than a week ago with a low-grade back strain, manager Dave Roberts revealed.
When he placed Henriquez on the injured list, Roberts was “hopeful” Henriquez would be back for the postseason.
The MRI, according to him, was “positive,” all things considered.
Thus far, things have played out accordingly, though the next week of recovery and rest will be the big test.
Why the Dodgers need Henriquez
Henriquez is the Dodgers’ most impressive right-handed reliever out of the bullpen.
He has a 2.62 ERA and a 2.50 FIP, and his profile is ideal for postseason baseball. He misses the barrel of the bat, strikes out hitters, and limits home runs, with command being the determining factor in his outing go.
Luckily for the Dodgers, Henriquez has figured out his control well enough that it hasn’t been a problem this year.
Compared to Edwin Diaz, Henriquez is much more reliable, while Brock Stewart and Evan Phillips are better suited for middle-relief chances.
If healthy, Henriquez should get save chances, with Roki Sasaki and Tanner Scott right in the mix as well. Diaz has started to creep up in the mix, but Henriquez has the confidence and demeanor to take command of the role.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — If there are any messages being sent this week, they’re subtle ones.
The Dodgers and Padres have become quite the rivalry in recent years. The Padres’ stars, particularly Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado, get on the nerves of Dodger fans. San Diegans, with their tendency to dislike all things associated with the metropolis to the north – except for that segment of folks who still can’t totally let go of the Chargers – relish the opportunity to, well, beat L.A.
Consider: When the Padres finally slew the dragon from the north as the late Peter Seidler, then owner, memorably predicted, they did everything but push back closing time in the Gaslamp Quarter. The roar that accompanied that 2022 National League Division Series victory might still be echoing in Petco Park all these years later, so hungry were Padres fans to take down the Dodgers, especially after L.A. had beaten them on neutral ground in the 2020 COVID-19-influenced postseason.
It’s also fairly obvious that the Dodgers’ 2022 failure, followed by a 2023 NLDS sweep by the Arizona Diamondbacks, helped create the monster in Chavez Ravine that is currently terrorizing all of baseball, including the segment of ownership that is willing to push the game to the brink in its zeal for a salary cap that labor has no intention of ever accepting.
You think Andrew Friedman and the rest of the Dodgers’ front office didn’t redouble their efforts following those two playoff flameouts? The mere possibility of a three-peat now should be proof of how much those losses stung. And the hype video in Dodger Stadium these nights is a pretty accurate representation of the state of mind here, the feeling that the Dodgers and their fans not only don’t care that they’ve become baseball’s villains, they relish it.
As the voiceover narrator puts it, “What’s wrong with being the bad guy? If being the best makes you bad, so be it. … If we’re being honest, sometimes it’s fun to root for the bad guy. … You need teams like us so you can point your finger and say, ‘That’s the bad guy.’”
The villainy works both ways, of course. Witness the first inning of the first game of this current series on Tuesday night.
Machado provokes strong reactions in L.A. because (a) he spent the final months of the 2018 season with the Dodgers, (b) his style of play was, shall we say, overly energy efficient – or, as he put it, “I’m not the type of player that’s going to be ‘Johnny Hustle’” – and (c) after that season he signed a 10-year, $300 million free agent contract with San Diego.
So, in Game 1 on Tuesday night, Brock Stewart’s first pitch to Machado knocked him down. The crowd jeered, loudly, and Machado took the moment to sit there and nod his head as if to say, “Yeah, it’s on.”
There were no further dust-ups in the first two games of this series, a 7-0 Dodgers victory on Tuesday night and a 5-1 Padres victory on Wednesday.
This wasn’t quite on the order of the series in June 2025, when then-Padres manager Mike Shildt and Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages exchanged words on the first night after Pages was hit by a pitch, Tatis and Shohei Ohtani were both plunked and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts was eventually ejected the second night, and Roberts and Shildt exchanged words at home plate after Tatis was hit again in Game 3.
Actually, the teams have been comparatively sedate in 2026. As for their fans on social media … ah, we’ll leave that alone.
But a Dodgers-Padres postseason series would almost certainly bring all of the emotions to the surface. Remember, the Padres not only knocked the Dodgers off in 2022 but had them on the ropes in 2024, one game away from another early elimination, before an 8-0 victory in a Game 4 bullpen game in San Diego reversed the momentum.
Also, keep in mind that after the Padres had knocked out Clayton Kershaw in an early season game in San Diego in 2023, a “Crying Kershaw” meme was posted on the Petco Park scoreboard. Consider, too, that the Dodgers gave fans replica Kershaw World Series rings before the first game of this series.
Coincidence? I think not.
And so here we are again. Los Angeles and San Diego split the first two games of their series this week, and while it might not be a major topic of conversation in either clubhouse this week you can bet these teams are casting wary eyes at each other, aware that fate could throw them together in yet another best-of-five (or maybe even best-of-seven) classic.
First things first. After Wednesday night’s game the Dodgers were still one victory or one Atlanta defeat away from clinching the No. 2 spot among division winners and the right to skip the best-of-three Wild Card round. The Padres’ magic number for clinching a wild card berth, likewise, was one.
Will Smith wasn’t about to look ahead. “We’re still approaching it as trying to win some ballgames,” he said. “I don’t think we’ve clinched the bye yet, so we’re still trying to do that.”
But Roberts acknowledged that it was in the back of his mind.
“Yeah, yeah, it’s in there,” he said.
“We’re pretty familiar with these guys. But yeah, absolutely. You know, we’re gathering information on Robbie Ray (Wednesday night’s starter), and, you know, there are guys in the ’pen and (Michael) King (Monday) and we’ll see (Nick) Pivetta (Thursday). So, certainly.”
And, Roberts noted before Wednesday night’s game in response to a question from San Diego Union-Tribune columnist Tom Krasovic, “They’re a thorn in our side and great competition.”
The feeling, I’m sure, is mutual. And while it might wear both teams out, don’t you wish these teams went back to facing each other 18 times during the regular season instead of 13, as they did this season?
Come to think of it, a five-game playoff series … nah, let’s not get too far ahead of ourselves.
jalexander@scng.com

item.content:encoded:
With the regular season winding down, the Los Angeles Dodgers have used bullpen days the last two games against the San Diego Padres and San Francisco Giants.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was originally the probable starter for Tuesday's game against San Diego, but the Dodgers are planning out a schedule to manage Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell, while also planning out their playoff rotation.
The back-up plan was to open with Roki Sasaki, who had missed almost a month due to a blister, but the youngster essentially re-wrote the lineup card.
“I said I wanted to pitch out of the bullpen,” Sasaki said per Dylan Hernandez of the New York Post. Rather than starting the game, Sasaki was inserted after a one inning each from Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski and Blake Treinen.
The 24-year-old righty pitched a scoreless fourth inning, and struck out two, but did allow two hits in his first outing since August 26th. It was Sasaki's first relief appearance since Game 6 of the World Series last year.
Dodgers' test run with Roki Sasaki was a success
Sasaki is clearly a prideful guy who wants to carve out a career as a starting pitcher. He was not thrilled about the move to the bullpen last season. Unlike many of his teammates, Sasaki isn't signed to a monster contract and likely wants to continue to start games in order to bank a large extension or free agency contract down the road. However, he's clearly in the right state of mind at the moment...perhaps unlike the Dodgers?
It's a little strange that the Dodgers were not planning to deploy Sasaki in relief of this game originally, right? He hadn't come out of the bullpen all season, and baseball players are as routine-oriented as human beings come. It's a little strange, but Sasaki clearly is locked in heading into October.
Sasaki appeared in nine postseason games last year. Sasaki has now appeared in 12 career games as a reliever including both the regular season and postseason, and the Dodgers are 12-0 in those games.
Sasaki has has a 0.66 ERA, 12:5 K:BB, and three saves in just over 13 innings of relief. The hopes are that a rejuvenated and healthy Sasaki can give this shaky, injury-riddled bullpen some stability before a possible three-peat.

item.content:encoded:
Tuesday night’s game against the San Diego Padres was reminiscent of the 2024 playoffs when the Dodgers were forced to employ a bullpen in the NLDS to keep their playoff hopes alive against those same Padres. Both outcomes were the same, with the bullpen shutting down the Friars and getting a big win.
That postseason saw a lot of bullpen usage, and in this one the Dodgers are stacked with starters. Still, the bullpen is always a big part of the postseason.
As Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic points out, 41 days ago manager Dave Roberts was asking the media what choices did he truly have to deploy in the ninth inning of games. Now, he could have several options.
Edwin Diaz, the closer they paid handsomely in the offseason, has not had a great season. He’s been on the IL twice and had an era over 11.00 at one point this summer. But since returning from his latest IL stint, he has faced 11 batters, struck out six and only allowed two to reach base.
“I think it’s one of those things where if you’re one of the 12 pitchers on a postseason roster, you’re in the trust tree,” Roberts said “He’s put himself right smack in that conversation. Given all that he’s had to go through this year to right the ship is a big credit to him.”
Roki Sasaki is also someone who will be in the mix for the ninth inning spot. He has also just returned from his own IL stint, pitching with dermabond on his blister. He allowed two singles, but worked around them for a scoreless inning in Tuesday night’s game. He will appear in Friday night’s game as he continues to work towards a spot in the bullpen that will likely vary as the postseason goes on.
Tanner Scott has been the Dodgers’ most reliable arm out of the bullpen this season, and Roberts has remarked how it would be nice to be able to use Scott in high leverage spots that may not come just in the ninth inning.
“I think if there’s an opportunity, for example, for Tanner to pitch a high-leverage inning in the seventh or the eighth inning, it’s just hard to pass that up if he’s the best option right there,” Roberts said. “You just don’t know where the ninth inning is going to be.”
Roberts also added that the team is sitting in their best position with regards to the bullpen as they have ever been. Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart round out the current options, and the team hopes that Edguardo Henriquez can recover from his back issues to appear in the playoffs. With the starters this team has overall this may be the best pitching staff the Dodgers have ever sent to the playoffs.

item.title: [FantasyPros] Brock Stewart breezes through spotless frame in win
item.dc:creator: Chase Davis
item.description: by Chase Davis | Dodgers Correspondent | Brock Stewart struck out one batter while allowing one hit in a scoreless opening inning during Tuesday's win over the Padres. Fantasy Impact: After Tuesday's win, Stewart now has a 2.45 ERA and 0.97 WHIP with one save and eight holds across 27 appearances. He served as the opener in a bullpen game with the Dodgers' playoff spot already clinched. Category: Game Recaps | More Brock Stewart: News, Rankings, Projections, Stats

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Last year at this time, Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart were both recovering from surgeries and unavailable to pitch. They were around the team but unable to contribute during the stretch run and postseason. This year, both veteran right-handers are two key cogs in an increasingly deep Dodgers bullpen and an important part of their October puzzle.
Phillips had Tommy John surgery in June 2025, wiping out the last half of last season and the first half of this one. When he returned from the injured list in July, the Dodgers were cautious in his usage, not using him on back-to-back days for his first four weeks, and used him on one day rest only four times during that stretch.
The results were spotty at first, allowing runs in five of his first seven appearances, including an uncharacteristic four home runs in such a short span. Since then, Phillips has allowed runs in only three of his last 21 appearances, and the lone home run surrendered was last Monday to Elly De La Cruz, which seems to be a rite of passage for everybody these days.
“Evan as you would expect, the first handful of outings were inconsistent coming off Tommy John, but I’d say the last [few] have been kind of who he is, and it’s been fun to see,” manager Dave Roberts said recently. “There’s a two-seamer, there’s a four-seamer, and some sweepers getting some awkward swings, some chase. That’s been good, and his command has been a lot better, too.”
Phillips in his 28 games has 28 strikeouts against only three unintentional walks. Since the start of August, the Dodgers have used Phillips more aggressively, pitching on back-to-back days five times, and he pitched three times in four days in three different stretches, and during that span has a 2.30 ERA and 2.46 FIP.
“I appreciate what they’ve done, trying to build me up, plus also protect me, plus giving me advantageous lanes while also challenging me,” Phillips said. “It’s been great so far, and I definitely feel like I’m coming closer and closer to that best version of myself that I have been and continue to strive to be.”
Stewart, a sixth-round draft pick of the Dodgers in 2014, was reacquired by the team at the 2025 trade deadline, but he pitched in only four games for them before succumbing to right shoulder debridement surgery in September. This year the right-hander has a 2.45 ERA and 2.53 xERA in his 27 games, with 24 strikeouts and seven unintentional walks in 25 2/3 innings, including a scoreless first inning to start Tuesday night’s bullpen-game shutout of the San Diego Padres.
“When Brock’s healthy, he’s as good as anyone we have,” Roberts said Tuesday. “For us, it’s just trying to manage him the right way and keep him strong and healthy. He’s been great.”
“That’s very cool to hear. I just go out there and throw it, that’s literally all I focus on. But people tell me that my — you know, I throw five pitches, which helps as a reliever,” Stewart said. “They tell me my stuff is pretty good, and it’s always nice to hear that. But I don’t know, I just go out there and throw it, try to compete as best I can, and hope it works out.
Roberts wasn’t wrong. Since returning to the majors in 2023 with the Minnesota Twins, Stewart has a 2.45 ERA and 2.78 xERA, which ranks 10th and ninth, respectively, among the 576 major league pitchers with at least 100 innings over the last four years. Tarik Skubal, with two Cy Young Awards during that stretch, has a 2.50 ERA and 2.73 xERA, for example.
But staying on the field has been a problem for Stewart, who this season alone has been on the injured list three different times — recovering from shoulder surgery, bone spur in his left foot, and shoulder discomfort — inactive for a total of 95 games. Since 2023, Stewart has also been on the injured list with elbow soreness, shoulder tendinitis, a shoulder strain, a hamstring strain, and shoulder inflammation, limited to just 106 2/3 total innings over the last four seasons.
“I feel good, but I’ve told everybody though, one day at a time. I’ve been hurt a lot so I always try to take things one day at a time. But I’m happy with the way I feel, happy with the way I felt today,” Stewart said. “Getting close to the finish line, but happy with how I feel, happy with how the stuff is coming out. I feel like I’m in a good spot and can hopefully help out.”
Stewart has pitched in the postseason only once, in three games over two series with the Minnesota Twins in 2023. Phillips was an October stalwart for the Dodgers since he was acquired on a waiver claim in 2021. In 12 appearances for the Dodgers in the playoffs, Phillips has yet to allow a run, over 15 1/3 innings, with 21 strikeouts and six unintentional walks. Phillips missed out on the World Series in 2024 with a right rotator cuff injury suffered during the NLCS, and was sidelined for all of last October.
“I love pitching in the postseason, I love competing with these guys. In 2024, missing out on the World Series, but I tried to dig in on the fact that I helped us get there, and played quite a large part in the Division Series and Championship Series. Obviously I want to see it all to the end, and help us carry that trophy off the field,” Philips said. “I’m just as eager as ever. Fortunate that I feel healthy at this time, and just trying to build on that, continue to chip away, and be the best I can when it matters most.”
This season, only Tanner Scott, Edwin Díaz, and Alex Vesia have a higher average-leverage index than Phillips and Stewart among Dodgers relievers. Phillips and Stewart have each saved a game this year, and Phillips has done so in the past with 46 saves with the Dodgers. Roberts said he’d feel comfortable with either Phillips or Stewart getting a save opportunity in October, along with a group that includes Tanner Scott and the just-activated Roki Sasaki.
“This year, more than any other year, I think there’s more guys we feel comfortable closing out games,” Roberts said.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers score 5 two-out runs off Padres starter Michael King in 7-0 victory
Tommy Edman and Will Smith homered as the Los Angeles Dodgers scored six runs with two outs to beat the San Diego Padres 7-0 in a series opener between rivals with the two best records in the majors this month
LOS ANGELES -- Tommy Edman and Will Smith homered as the Los Angeles Dodgers scored six runs with two outs to beat the San Diego Padres 7-0 on Tuesday night in a series opener between rivals with the two best records in the majors this month.
The Dodgers (97-60) moved within one game of NL Central champion Milwaukee (98-59) for the top mark in the big leagues and home-field advantage throughout the postseason. However, the Brewers own the head-to-head tiebreaker.
Los Angeles needs one win or an Atlanta loss to clinch a first-round bye into a National League Division Series.
The NL West champion Dodgers improved to 15-5 in September with their fifth straight victory; the Padres fell to 14-5 and had their five-game winning streak snapped.
San Diego is tied with Chicago and Philadelphia at 87-70 for the three NL wild cards — four games ahead of Arizona with five to play.
Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado were a combined 1 for 7 with five strikeouts for the Padres.
The Dodgers chased Michael King (12-10) after four innings in his career-high 32nd start of the season. The right-hander gave up five runs on six hits and struck out five as his four-game winning streak ended.
Los Angeles broke out with four runs in the second. King got the first two outs on six pitches before loading the bases. Teoscar Hernández and rookie Josue De Paula hit consecutive singles before King plunked Andy Pages, who just came off the injured list.
King then issued back-to-back walks to Edman and Mookie Betts, forcing in two runs. Freddie Freeman's two-run single made it 4-0.
Betts had a ground-rule double and scored on Freeman's two-out single for a 5-0 lead in the fourth.
Edman's solo shot came with two outs in the sixth and Smith added a 396-foot drive with one out in the seventh for a 7-0 lead.
Brock Stewart started a bullpen game and Justin Wrobleski (12-5) got the win for the Dodgers, who used eight pitchers to earn the fifth shutout in franchise history when deploying at least that many.
Among them was reliever Edwin Díaz, who struck out two in one inning. Roki Sasaki's four-seam fastball touched 100 mph while he pitched one inning. The Japanese right-hander came off the injured list earlier Tuesday after missing nearly a month with a blister on his right middle finger.
Padres LHP Robbie Ray (13-8, 3.60 ERA) starts Wednesday against Dodgers RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-8, 2.51).
___
This story has been corrected to show the Dodgers scored six runs with two outs, not five.

item.content:encoded:
Last year, the Dodgers hardly used their bullpen in the playoffs.
This year, they would like that to once again be the blueprint.
In their bid to three-peat as World Series champions, of course, the Dodgers are expected to be led by their star-studded rotation. Shohei Ohtani isn’t pitching, but Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow are.
And if all goes according to plan, they will handle the bulk of the innings.
However, replicating the starting pitching excellence of last October won’t be easy. A season ago, the Dodgers’ four-man rotation of Ohtani, Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow accounted for 113 of the team’s 165 postseason innings (including relief appearances from Glasnow and Yamamoto). Together, they posted a 2.55 ERA.
It was historic production.
Which also means, it’s fair to assume some regression will be possible –– both in workload and effectiveness.
Thus, having more reliable bullpen options this time around could be equally important for the Dodgers. And while that might have felt like a daunting reality earlier this year, when the unit was banged up and struggling through the middle portion of the campaign, Tuesday night was a reminder that the relief corps could be a strength in this fall’s title pursuit.
“Obviously we’ve had a lot of talent over the years,” manager Dave Roberts said. “But as far as sitting here today at the end of the season, it’s as good of shape as we’ve ever been in with the bullpen.”
In a 7-0 win over the San Diego Padres, the Dodgers were not supposed to have the pitching matchup –– countering Padres ace Michael King with a makeshift bullpen game in a rivalry series opener at Dodger Stadium.
Instead, eight different Dodgers relievers held the previous red-hot Padres to a five-hit shutout. Along the way, several arms who once seemed like question marks continued to round into increasingly promising form.
“It was fantastic,” Roberts said. “This is as good as our bullpen has been, has thrown.”
It started with opener Brock Stewart, a key right-handed weapon in the Dodgers’ bullpen who began the game with a scoreless first inning, continuing his late-season resurgence after another injury-plagued year.
From there, the baton was passed on down.
Justin Wrobleski, who is in the midst of a late-season conversion to the bullpen for the second-straight year, escaped a jam in the second. Blake Treinen, who might be on the postseason roster bubble given the Dodgers’ relief depth, offered one of his best outings of late by issuing only a two-out walk in a scoreless third.

The highlight of the night came in the fourth and fifth, when Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz hung a couple more zeroes in what were important appearances from each.
For Sasaki, the outing marked his first since returning from the injured list and making his own late-season move back to the bullpen, where he could reprise his role as closer from last year’s playoffs. He worked around a pair of singles with two strikeouts and a fastball that, even after being sidelined for the last month by a blister, sat at 99-100 mph.
For Díaz, Tuesday was not only a third-consecutive scoreless outing since his own return from the IL, but his most impressive yet as he makes a bid for the playoff roster. He retired the top of the Padres lineup in order with a pair of strikeouts, and has now retired 9 of 11 batters he has faced since rejoining the active roster.
Asked postgame if Díaz –– the $69 million offseason signing who lost the closer’s job amid a previously dismal debut Dodgers season –– could still pitch his way back into ninth-inning duties, Roberts said it’s “certainly possible.”
“The way he’s throwing, the ninth is possible, yes,” Roberts added.
By that point, the Dodgers had already pulled away from the Padres. They mounted a four-run rally with two outs in the second against King, who issued back-to-back bases-loaded walks to Tommy Edman and Mookie Betts before Freddie Freeman slashed a two-run single through the infield. The offense tacked on more runs in the fourth (on another Freeman RBI single), the sixth (on a solo home run from Tommy Edman), and the seventh (a Will Smith solo blast).
In what was the lineup’s toughest test in a while, they passed with flying colors.
Still, the night’s most encouraging developments came from the ‘pen, which capped off the game with two scoreless innings from Kyle Hurt, then stress-free appearances in the eighth and ninth from Alex Vesia and Jack Dreyer.
The unit’s most trusted arms at the moment, Tanner Scott (who figures to be vying with Sasaki for the postseason closer role) and Evan Phillips, weren’t even required. Nor was Edgardo Henriquez, who remains sidelined by a back injury but still could return in time for the playoffs.
“We know we have a good group, and anytime we get to carry the load and everybody has success and throws up zeros, it’s special,” Stewart said. “That’s really hard to do, for all eight guys or whatever it was today. So yeah, it’s cool.”
With a smirk, he added: “Write stories about it.”
Come October, of course, the Dodgers will be hoping their relievers are the main story.
But if the rotation falters, the club seems significantly better-suited to handle it than it did a year ago.
“That could change in a day, in a game, as we all know,” Roberts said. “But right now, feel really good about everyone out there.”

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Roki Sasaki could pitch his way into the Los Angeles Dodgers’ closer conversation before the postseason begins.
Manager Dave Roberts confirmed Tuesday that using Sasaki as a closer in October is an option, although the Dodgers have not assigned him the ninth inning—or any fixed relief role—as he returns from the injured list.
“It’s certainly an option,” Roberts said. “A lot of it probably is contingent on how he throws here tonight.”
Sasaki was activated with Andy Pages before the Dodgers opened their series against the San Diego Padres. Rather than returning to the rotation, the right-hander will spend the final week auditioning for a postseason bullpen role.
Dodgers will evaluate Sasaki in multiple roles
Roberts said Sasaki could work two innings in his first appearance, entering at the start of a clean inning. That opportunity could arrive early, in the middle innings or late in the game depending on how the matchup develops.
“I could envision him pitching multiples,” Roberts said. “I can see him coming into a clean inning and pitching two innings. I’m not sure if that’s the third inning or the sixth inning or the eighth inning, but he’s ready.”
The Dodgers then expect to give Sasaki one or two shorter appearances before the regular season ends. Those outings will help determine whether he can handle a traditional closing assignment, provide multiple innings or fill another high-leverage role in October.
Roberts stopped short of labeling Sasaki the closer and noted that his late-inning success last season developed from the Dodgers’ needs at the time.
“I don’t want to say he’s going to finish games or be a closer,” Roberts said. “Last year was one of those things where it was a situation of need, as far as where we were at with performance, with health of guys, and he filled that role admirably.”
Dodgers do not have a designated closer
Sasaki’s opportunity comes as the Dodgers prepare to enter October without one reliever locked into the ninth inning. Roberts said he would prefer a set closer in a perfect scenario, but he does not currently see one pitcher holding that job.
“Right now, I don’t see a one-person closer,” Roberts said.
That approach would allow Roberts to deploy Tanner Scott against the most dangerous portion of an opponent’s lineup before the ninth rather than saving him for a lead that might never materialize. Roberts also said he would be comfortable asking Evan Phillips or Brock Stewart to close a game.
Phillips has looked more like himself over his last three appearances following an inconsistent beginning to his return from Tommy John surgery, according to Roberts. Stewart has also been one of the Dodgers’ most effective relievers when healthy.
The Dodgers therefore have several ninth-inning possibilities. Sasaki’s final regular-season appearances will determine whether he becomes one of their most prominent options.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are opening up for a blockbuster series, their last big test, against the San Diego Padres.
Dodgers Lineup
1. Mookie Betts, SS
2. Freddie Freeman, 1B
3. Will Smith, C
4. Max Muncy, 3B
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
7. Josue De Paula, DH
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Tommy Edman, 2B
Andy Pages is back in the batting order after being activated from the injured list. He broke his hand after getting hit by a pitch, had surgery, and after a month on the shelf, he is back.
It may take some time for him to shake off the rust at the plate, but his defense should not skip a beat.
The Dodgers are facing righty Michael King, but many of the hottest bats are righties.
Mookie Betts, Will Smith, and Kyle Tucker are among the most dialed-in hitters, and they should drive most of the offense.
Ideally, Freddie Freeman gets going again, since he hasn’t looked right in a while.
Who’s pitching for the Dodgers
The Dodgers will have Brock Stewart as the opener, with Roki Sasaki getting the bulk of the work out of the bullpen.
On Tuesday, hours before the game, Sasaki was activated off the injured list after recovering from his blister.
Sasaki has been great since the All-Star break, posting a 3.05 ERA with 37 strikeouts and 15 walks.
His splitter and slider are fantastic, while the fastball has been the difference-maker, showing some renewed life.
The Japanese righty is set to enter the bullpen in a varied role, either stepping in for a struggling starter or pitching late in high-leverage spots.
Stewart, meanwhile, has been a bit lucky, with a 2.55 ERA and a 3.91 FIP.
FanGraphs’ pitching models have appreciated his stuff and command, and while he has pitched better lately, he is prone to giving up hard contact.

item.content:encoded:
Ninth inning. Trumpets blaring. Edwin Díaz trotting out of the bullpen to collect the final three outs of a game.
It’s a scene the Dodgers dreamt about all winter, after signing the star closer to a $69 million contract in December.
It’s become an all-too-rare occurrence since then, with the right-hander battling injuries and underperformance in what has been a nightmarish debut season.
Yet, last Friday night, such a moment materialized again in Díaz’s return from the injured list — helping set the stage for a crucial final week in which the right-hander will battle for a place on the Dodgers’ postseason roster.
“I gotta show them I’m part of that bullpen,” Díaz said. “I haven’t pitched [much] this year, and when I’ve been on the mound, I’ve been struggling. So right now I’m giving my 200% just to show them I will be in that roster spot … Just every time, when they give me the ball in any situation, I will do my job.”
Granted, Friday’s outing wasn’t a save opportunity, with Díaz only pitching because the Dodgers held a comfortable six-run lead. Neither was his appearance in another rout of the Giants on Saturday, with the Dodgers continuing to ease him back in lower-leverage situations.
Still, at this point of the year, Díaz’s pair of scoreless innings were nonetheless signs of progress.
“I liked everything,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I liked his intensity. I liked the fastball velocity. The slider was good. So it was just really good to kind of get him back in the mix. That’s something to build on.”
Over this final week, the Dodgers will need to see more such outings. If Díaz is to make their postseason roster, he can no longer afford any bouts of regression.
“I just want to keep climbing the ladder,” Díaz said, “and finish the season strong.”
That Díaz is even in this spot is a reminder of all the ways his highly anticipated debut Dodgers season has gone wrong.
He stumbled through the opening month, suffering an ERA above 10.00, before being diagnosed with loose bodies in his elbow that required a surgical procedure.
When he returned in late July, his results still didn’t improve, with the 32-year-old giving up 11 more runs in nine more frustrating outings while continuing to battle flaws in his delivery.
Another injured list stint came in late August, when Díaz was shut down again with inflammation in his neck.
During that absence, he and the team tried to clean up his mechanics — specifically identifying a drop in his arm angle as a potential root cause of his problems this year. Yet, in his first four outings of a minor-league rehab assignment, he gave up six runs (including five in one disastrous appearance on Sept. 13) and walked seven batters.
As a result, just last week, Roberts openly cast doubt on Díaz’s postseason roster chances.

However, Díaz went back to the drawing board one more time during his stint in Triple-A. This time, he sat down with the club’s Oklahoma City pitching coaches, Ryan Dennick and David Anderson, to review old video from his three-time All-Star career.
That process yielded a new solution, with the trio finding that Díaz “wasn’t moving my hips the [same] way” he had in previous seasons.
Thus, Díaz made an adjustment in a bullpen session last week, looked good enough in one final rehab outing to be brought back to the majors and at least showed some signs of promise in his back-to-back outings last weekend — specifically by commanding his fastball better and allowing his slider to play off it deceptively.
“I’ve been able to throw strikes,” Díaz said, after striking out four batters and allowing just one hit and one walk in the two appearances. “I think that was my problem. I wasn’t throwing my fastball for strikes. Now I’m able to command my fastball really good. When I command my fastball, my slider plays up. So I feel really good right now.”
More improvement will be required, of course, if Díaz is to still salvage a spot on the team’s postseason roster.
He has already lost the closer role. He is battling with a slew of other right-handers, such as Blake Treinen and Brock Stewart, just for a middle relief gig.
It certainly isn’t what the Dodgers expected when they signed him in what felt like a coup back in December.
All they can hope for now is that, if the trumpets blare again in October, he has made enough progress to at least give them something out of the bullpen.
“It’s tough,” Díaz said. “But at the same time, I’m always positive. I know when I click, I click.”
